subtopic: POSTAGE STAMPS
POSTAGE STAMPS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT ON ELIMINATION OF CORNER BLOCKS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a brief announcement in connection with stamps. The previous administration decided early this year to eliminate certain identifying marks known as plate numbers on the corner of each sheet of postage stamps sold. While this action was designed to avoid confusion and delays in the public sale of stamps by those collectors who desired special selections to be made by post office clerks, it had the unfortunate effect of denying to those same people the opportunity of pursuing their hobby of collecting corner plate blocks of stamps.
I have been impressed by the representations from these collectors and others, and in accordance with the government's policy of operating as efficiently as possible while still giving due weight to the interests of those who are affected by government action, I have decided on an amendment to the decision of the previous government in this matter.
Therefore, while plate numbers will no longer appear on those sheets of stamps sold at post offices throughout the country, thus eliminating a cause of annoyance and delay to those purchasing stamps for ordinary use, sheets bearing such a designation will be available for sale to any interested collector, at the face value of the stamps, through the philatelic section of the Post Office Department at Ottawa.
96698-168i
Since stamps are designed and printed a considerable time in advance of their issue, it will not be possible to apply this new treatment to certain issues designed by the previous administration which were too far advanced in production for it to be applied. However, the new system will enable all collectors who are interested in this branch of the philatelic hobby to continue their collections as in the past, and is yet another indication of the desire of the Post Office Department to offer satisfactory service to every Canadian.

speakeroldname: Hon. D. S. Harkness (Minisier of Agriculture) moved
subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 237, for the stabilization of the prices of agricultural commodities.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is the stage at which the general principle of the legislation before the house is debated. For this bill the principle is to establish a flexible agricultural price support program which will provide a guaranteed yearly price for any-and I should like to stress the word "any"-agricultural commodity for which such a guaranteed price may be required; and further, to provide an ultimate security feature which will ensure that, as far as nine key agricultural commodities are concerned, a mandatory floor will be in effect at all times. Both these levels of support are to be related to a moving average formula.
The guarantees provided to Canadian farmers by this bill are much greater than anything they have ever had before, and these guarantees are implicit in the bill. However, concern has been expressed by members of parliament of this party representing rural constituencies and by officials of farm organizations that these guarantees are not spelled out in sufficient detail in the bill, and that this omission has led to misunderstanding as to what the bill can and will do for our farmers.
In order to remove any doubts as to what is intended I am quite willing to spell out the guarantees which are implicit in the bill. To this end I have consulted officials of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and of the farm unions, and have asked them for their opinions and recommendations as to how they think the legislation can be improved within the general principle of the bill of providing a flexible price support system.
Having held these various consultations, I am prepared at the committee of the whole stage to move, or rather I should say to have moved, amendments along the following lines. First, the inclusion of a preamble in these words:
Whereas it is expedient to enact a measure for the purpose of stabilizing the prices of agricultural commodities in order to assist the industry of agriculture to realize fair returns for its labour and investment, and to maintain a fair relationship between prices received by farmers and the costs of the goods and services that they buy: Therefore-
And then comes the usual enactment phrase. This preamble has been put in so it will serve to indicate clearly the nature and purpose of the act, to the end that there

will be no ambiguity whatever as to what is intended by the act and what its purpose is.
Second, to add a new subsection to section 2 to read:
(2) In prescribing a percentage of the base price of an agricultural commodity under subparagraph (i) or (ii) of paragraph (e) of subsection (1), the governor in council shall have regard to the estimated average cost of production of the commodity, and such other factors as the governor in council considers to be relevant.
The addition of this new subsection will make it clear that the cost of production is the most important factor to be taken into consideration in setting the guaranteed annual price.
Third, in connection with the make-up of the advisory committee, I have been informed that some doubt existed because of the wording there, as to whether the members of that committee would be all farmers or representative of farm organizations. To remove any doubt along that line the proposal is to strike out the words "include representation from" and make the clause read:
5. (1) The minister shall appoint an advisory committee, consisting of a chairman and at least six, but not more than nine, other members, composed of farmers and representatives of farm organizations.
As I said, that change is in order to make it absolutely clear that the advisory committee will be made up of farmers or their representatives from farm organizations.
Fourth, to add to subclause (1) of clause 7 in order to make it read:
The board shall from time to time in accordance with this act take such action as is necessary to stabilize the prices of agricultural commodities at their respective prescribed prices-
And this is the part which is added:
-and shall take such action and make such recommendations as are necessary to ensure that the prescribed prices for an agricultural commodity in effect from time to time shall bear a fair relationship to the base price for such commodity.
This wording has been added in order to ensure that the guaranteed yearly prices will be at an adequate level.
In addition to the representations that the guarantees in regard to the annual guaranteed prices were not spelled out sufficiently, the advice I have received is that the use of the three-year moving average as the means of determining the base price is viewed with disfavour at the present time because the prices during the past three years have not been satisfactory. As far as the general principle of this bill is concerned, it does not matter whether the formula used is the three-year moving average, a five-year moving average, or a ten-year moving average. I personally favour the three-year moving average formula, as I believe that over the
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization long term it would prove more satisfactory and provide greater assistance to farmers than a five or ten-year base period.
However, in view of the recommendations of the farm organizations, and because the use of a 10-year moving average will now include five years of the highest prices which farmers have received-that is the period from 1948 to 1952-the government is prepared to amend the bill to provide for the use of a 10-year moving average as the base period rather than the three-year moving average. All that is required to do is to substitute the word "ten" for the word "three" where it appears in section 8 of the bill.
I think it is apparent that the willingness we have shown to consult with farm organizations and to make amendments to improve the bill in line with their thinking shows that this government takes no hard and fast take it or leave it attitude in regard to this very important matter.

speechtext:
It demonstrates that we are prepared to go to any possible limit to meet the needs and desires of farmers within the general principle of putting into effect a flexible support system which will be practical and workable.
The general position taken by the right hon. member for Melville (Mr. Gardiner) and the Liberal party at the resolution stage of this legislation was that it does no more for the farmers than the Agricultural Prices Support Act which they introduced, and is probably not as good. I do not think any farmer who studies this legislation will agree with that contention.
There are, in particular, four very important differences between this legislation and the legislation we have had in effect so far. First of all, this legislation provides a formula to serve as a basis for setting support prices, and it will be possible to get some system into the type of support prices and the level of those support prices which have been set. Under the present legislation the comparatively small number of products which were put under price support were put on the level provided for them on an entirely ad hoc basis, and those supports were put on one level for one commodity which bore no relationship whatever to that put on for another commodity.
Second, this legislation provides quite definitely for an advisory committee, composed and representative of farmers, for the specific purpose of advising as to what commodities should be under price support and
2654	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization the level of the guaranteed yearly price to be provided for them. The old legislation did contain provision for the board to appoint an advisory committee, and there was in fact an advisory committee. That committee was not, however, for the specific purpose of advising the board in regard to price support legislation, but was a carry-over from an advisory committee which had existed during the war. It was under the price support board, apparently only for what you might call a lack of any other place to put it.
The committee which has been in existence consisted of the deputy ministers of agriculture of the various provinces and some representatives of farm organizations. It met twice a year as a rule, though sometimes only once a year. It met for two days, gave advice on general agricultural questions, discussed general agricultural problems, and then made certain recommendations to the government; but as I say, it was not a committee for the specific purpose of advising in regard to the commodities which should be under price support and the levels of those supports.
The third main difference between this legislation and what we have had previously is that it provides for a guaranteed yearly price to be set one year in advance. Once they are set they are to remain in effect for the following 12 months. The old legislation contained no such provision, and nothing along that line is really done under it. Very frequently a price support was set for two or three months or something along that line; otherwise it was just set and there was no term provided, and it could be cut off at any moment.
There has been a very strong demand on the part of the farmers that the level of price supports should be known to them; that they should know when the supports are going to be in effect and what the levels are going to be during that period so that they as farmers may plan their operations accordingly. This legislation makes that provision.
The fourth main difference is that this legislation provides an ultimate security feature. It provides for a mandatory floor at all times on nine key commodities. The old legislation provided for no mandatory floors at all, and was not comparable to or in line with this in any way whatsoever.
The C.C.F. and Social Credit groups at the resolution stage criticized this bill because it has no rigid formula. That, in effect, is what most of their criticism boiled down to. An examination of what has happened in the

At the time I was interrupted I was just going to quote certain statements made by the secretary of agriculture of the United States to indicate what great difficulties their rigid support system has got them into, and the desire which exists

in that country to get away from a rigid price support system. The quotation I just started to read is as follows:
The only way in which price support by rigid formula can be made to work-even in the short run-is by effective control over production, so that gluts in the market are rather quickly removed and supply is rapidly adjusted to what the market will take. We have no such control over production today.
That is in spite of the fact that they had very considerable controls as far as acreage quotas were concerned, and things of that sort. I do not think there is any farmer in this country who wants us to put into effect a system under which he is told how many acres of barley or any other commodity he can plant, or how much livestock he can raise of a particular kind. To put into effect and even attempt to make work a rigid system of price support, something along that line is necessary.
Mr. Benson went on and said:
Price supports "used in a manner that fits today's conditions" have an important function in agriculture, but that he does not believe in supports which price products out of markets, build up unmanageable surpluses and force controls on farmers which make their farms inefficient.
Stating that many people "have the false impression that most agricultural prices and incomes are government supported", he points out that items from "only 13 crops, plus dairy products and wool, are in government inventory-out of about 250 commodities that farmers produce". He adds that wheat and cotton account for over 48 per cent of price support costs. "Is it good for agriculture", he asks, "that more than four-fifths (82.2 per cent) of these price support costs should go to the producers of four commodities? Is it good for agriculture as a whole that nearly four-fifths (79 per cent) of these price support costs should go to about one-fourth of our farms?"
That is one of the further difficulties so far as a rigid price support system is concerned. You have a rigid formula which is laid down by law. You cannot alter it, and you get all kinds of anomalies. The way in which it has worked out over there, as he indicates, is that four-fifths of the money paid out for price supports has gone to only one-fourth of their farmers. Mr. Benson summarizes these various difficulties in two short statements, one of which appears on page 5 and the other a little later. These are his words in summarizing really the disadvantages of a rigid price support system:
I say again that price supports-used in a manner that fits today's conditions-do have an important function in agriculture.
We believe that, and that is why we have this bill before us at the present time. He goes on:
But I do not believe in price supports set at levels which price our products out of markets that farmers must have.
I do not believe in price supports which build up unmanageable surpluses that depress prices and cost millions to store.

No, I do not believe in price supports which force controls upon farmers, making their farms inefficient, and which chase acres out of one crop only to dump both the acres and surplus problems on other crops.
I can quite understand that the C.C.F. party does believe in this control. They are a party who believe in a socialized country and a socialized industry, and I can quite understand that they would like to have a socialized agriculture, and to have controls of all sorts as far as agriculture is concerned. But I do not think very many farmers in this country believe in it, and I am quite sure very few if any farmers would agree to acreage controls and to be told what they could plant, how much of it, and so forth.

What is the difference between "supporting" and "stabilizing"? "Stabilizing" is keeping them as they are and "supporting" is doing whatever is necessary in order to improve them. It was largely addressed to our friends over in the corner, the C.C.F. I want to point out that this is a rather new attitude on the part of the government party of today. The present government while in opposition joined with the C.C.F. in a number of activities. The one which was most spectacular was in their opposition to the pipe line; and one, of course, can understand the attitude taken with regard to that matter.
That, however, was only the final act in a well planned effort to defeat Liberalism. The co-operation was first evident in Saskatchewan following the election of 1940, when the Conservative provincial leader was elected to the House of Commons. The common practice was to join the C.C.F. in attacks upon the Liberals, both federally and provincially, and then on nomination day to withdraw most of their candidates and leave those opposed to the Liberals with only one choice. That was the plan of operation.
After they had met with considerable success as a result of these tactics in Saskatchewan, the idea was introduced into their plans to oust the Liberals from power in Ottawa. When the address in reply to the speech from the throne was under discussion the hon. member for Yorkton moved an amendment in these words, as reported at page 582 of Hansard of January 23, 1957:
We regret, however, that Your Excellency's advisers seem to favour a flexible price support program . . .
Of course it is obvious that His Excellency's advisers at that time were the Liberal government:
We regret, however, that Your Excellency's advisers seem to favour a flexible price support program, the effect of which is to leave the agricultural industry in a state of uncertainty and insecurity; we also regret that Your Excellency's advisers have failed to take the necessary steps to establish a system of parity prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure 100 per cent parity of income for agricultural producers.
It will be noted that two points were raised there. The first was intended to condemn flexible price support, and the second was to support 100 per cent of parity. When the vote was taken every Conservative who was in the house, including the leader of the official opposition, the then member for Prince Albert, voted against the amendment.

Well, I am coming to that. It should be noted here that when previous votes had been recorded there was a tendency for some persons not to be present at the time the vote was taken, but on this occasion most of those who had previously been absent were present, as the vote will show. On this occasion the official opposition were present to vote with the government, not with the C.C.F. In other words the position which had been taken on previous occasions had been altered, in that there was a direct vote. I presume if you can take a vote against an amendment to be in favour of something, there was a vote in favour of the flexible price which the government of the day had been putting into effect and there was, in the same way, a vote against 100 per cent of parity, which was a new position for one of the parties to have taken.
This gave rise to considerable cross-firing between the official opposition and the C.C.F. group which would be interesting if I had time to record it. I might say, however, one is not required to quote much to prove the position taken then by the present Prime Minister. He summarized the position in his speech on the amendment to the motion to
2666	HOUSE OF
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization go into supply in 1956, as reported at pages 2021 to 2023 of Hansard* He said:
The squeeze which the farmer suffers results from the disparity In the relationship between the prices of farm products and the prices the farmer has to pay. When they are in proper relationship parity is established, and it is parity that the farm organizations across this country are asking for today.
Later on the hon. member for Prince Albert said:
I know of no better definition of parity than that which appeared in yesterday's New York Times. I have made the necessary changes in the definition to meet the situation in this country. It is as follows:
"Parity prices are the dollars and cents prices that give to farm products the same buying or purchasing power they had in a selected base period when prices received by and prices paid by farmers were regarded as in good balance.
He illustrated by saying one should be able to buy the same quantity of necessities with a load of barley in each of those periods. The hon. member for Prince Albert again went on to say:
It goes on to point out-
He was referring to the article in the New York Times.
-the difference between rigid price supports which have not proved successful and flexible price supports which have proved successful in the experience of the United States.
He then continued to point out the number of times he had advocated parity prices, and he went back over the record which I have placed on Hansard today and said this, as reported at page 2023 of Hansard:
One of the earliest occasions was in 1941, during the war. The last occasion when we moved an amendment regarding this question of parity prices was on March 23, 1953.
I refer to that to come back to the statement I made earlier, namely that the words "parity prices" were not in that resolution moved at that time, but the present Prime Minister said later on, when reviewing it, that it was a motion in favour of parity prices. Then he said:
At that time I moved this amendment.
The amendment, as I have pointed out, does not have the words "parity prices" in it. The amendment reads:
That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
Since I have already put this resolution on the record I will not do it again. The present Prime Minister then argued that the Conservative platform of 1948 was intended to support parity prices. The present Prime Minister moved, seconded by the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton), the following motion, as reported at page 2024 of Hansard of 1956:


That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
"in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to create a parity of prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship.
In speaking to the amendment the hon. member for Prince Albert said, as reported at page 2026 of Hansard of March 12, 1956:
The trend referred to in the amendment moved in 1953 has continued. Canadian agriculture today would not be in its present precarious position if action had been taken at that time on the basis of the experience of our neighbour to the south and also on the basis of the demands of farmers generally.
There can be no question, then, that what the present Prime Minister had in mind when he was playing along with the C.C.F. was parity prices as they had them in the United States down to 1953. On each occasion when the hon. member for Prince Albert moved such an amendment to the motion to go into supply I rose and said we had two reasons for opposing it. First, we were opposed to the United States system of parity price support and, second, it was a trick motion to put our candidates in wrong in agricultural constituencies.
We were not surprised when in January, 1957, the C.C.F. called their hand, and we found the Conservative party had so acted as to cause their leader to follow Conservative rather than C.C.F. doctrine.
But what happened when the Prime Minister got into the election campaign? He was naturally speaking in the larger centres and always through the larger dailies to the people who were opposed to 100 per cent parity prices which had been attempted in the United States. He was reported in the Winnipeg Free Press as having said on May 14:
The price support system advanced by the Conservatives would feature a flexible formula. Critics of support prices said they would create huge surpluses such as those which had developed in the United States from the support system there. The difference was, Mr. Diefenbaker said, that the program proposed by his party would be based on a flexible formula, the United States surpluses had developed because of a fixed formula.
The following day in the Winnipeg Free Press and other dailies he was reported to have said:
The C.C.F. in the last session of parliament had called for 100 per cent parity price support for agriculture. "What nonsense". Did anyone believe that the people of Canada would permit the taxation necessary to give farmers their full pay regardless of production?
He went on to use an illustration following that, and asked if a labourer should be paid

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
full prices when he came under unemployment insurance. Should he be given his full pay, and therefore should the farmer be given his full pay?
A few days later, on May 18, he is reported in the Regina Leader-Post as saying:
I urged a system of parity prices in 1941 in a resolution in the house, and asked for it two other times. But every Liberal voted against it. This year I moved a resolution for a price support program to allow a fair cost relationship. That's what the farmers want, not the 100 per cent parity prices the C.C.F. asks which I voted against because I knew it was a trick motion. The Liberals voted my motion down again.
As I pointed out, every one of those resolutions except one was on a motion to go into supply and therefore a trick motion. The one which was not on a motion to go into supply was on the address. The recorded vote on the one on the address is in Hansard to be looked at by anyone to corroborate what I have been saying. During the campaign, in speaking to the audiences I have mentioned, the Prime Minister made the statements to which I have referred. At least he is reported to have made them, and I presume the reports are correct; I have not heard of them being corrected.
Then what was being said throughout the rural press of western Ontario? Candidates were carrying advertisements based on the Prime Minister's previous statement in the house claiming that he was for 100 per cent parity. If anyone doubts that, though I am sure there are members on the other side of the house who know it is correct, all they need to do is look at the advertisements. I have one of them here. What does that advertisement say? It was issued on June 5, 1957 in the Chatham Daily News. It says:
Mr. Consumer says: "Our cost of living continues to rise with lower farm prices". What is the answer?
I may say there is something just as interesting in the upper part of this advertisement, but I am not going to take time to read it because it does not strictly refer to the question under discussion.
What is the answer? John Diefenbaker and Albert Jolley say 100 per cent parity support prices. Protection from American subsidized surpluses. Regain foreign markets. Diefenbaker tax policy. Diefenbaker monetary policy. A vote for Albert Jolley is a vote for John Diefenbaker.
The only point to which I wish to draw attention at the moment is that the very first item mentioned in that advertisement is 100 per cent parity support prices. I can quite understand, Mr. Speaker, why there have been some changes in the legislation as it was first brought down. I can understand why some members from the rural areas of Ontario, who were elected on the strength
of these advertisements, were insisting on some changes being made in the bill as it was first brought before this house.
I want to say to those members that the amendments which have been made, and which have been introduced today, are not sufficient to meet the criticism they are going to receive when they go back home after this session as a result of having appealed for votes and succeeded on the basis of these advertisements. I understand these advertisements were placed generally all through agricultural sections of the east and some of them, probably not quite so strong as that, in some of the newspapers in the west.
What did the Minister of Agriculture say about this when speaking on the resolution? The minister spoke on Wednesday, December 11, 1957, and at page 2186 of Hansard we find this:
However, what was generally in mind was some sort of system such as that in effect in the United States-
That is, when people were talking about parity prices that was what most of them had in their minds.
-because our farmers were aware that men across the border in the same lines of production as themselves in many cases were receiving higher prices.
At the same time it was common knowledge amongst all who had studied the matter at all that the United Strates parity price system had led to difficulties of various kinds.
Apparently the leader of the Conservative party of that day had not made any studies, because on several occasions and right until he became leader of the Conservative party he had advocated the adoption of that particular system. The Minister of Agriculture went on to say:
It had resulted in the accumulation of vast surpluses of many agricultural products which had proven embarrassing to the United States agricultural economy and government, and the disposal of which has had serious effects on Canada and other nations.
I think it was about at that point that the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre rose on a point of order to ascertain whether or not his system was working properly.

In view of all this, as a first step in attempting to devise a practical and workable agricultural prices stabilization bill for Canada I took a fairly close look at the United States system with a view to determining the defects in that system so we might avoid the difficulties which they have run into.
The first and most important defect, I believe, is the lack of flexibility and from this cause most of their troubles have developed.
Now, I just refer back to the resolution which was put on the record to the effect that the C.C.F. party did not believe in flexibility. They apparently do not believe in flexibility even now, judging from what we have heard during the discussion of this question. I can quite understand why the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre thought there was something wrong with the loudspeaker system. Up to this point the speech delivered by the Minister of Agriculture could have been quoted from my speeches when I was trying to keep his leader on the right track on other occasions. I would not have been surprised if the minister had said at that point, "We have therefore decided to continue on the statute books the most flexible plan ever devised, that is the present Agricultural Prices Support Act."
Instead, he proceeded to suggest changes, every one of which I suggest rendered the new plan less flexible than the old one. Everything which can be done under this measure could be done under the old act. We did select a group of commodities under which we placed supports. The act was so flexible that it was possible to deal with cattle while the foot-and-mouth disease was prevalent and take them out again when it would have done harm to deal with them any longer.
In other words, there is nothing in the act which said we were going to deal with foot-and-mouth disease under this legislation. No one had any idea that foot-and-mouth disease was going to develop, but this legislation is sufficiently flexible that we were able to step in and deal with the problems which resulted from the fact that there had been foot-and-mouth disease in this country, and when it became necessary to get rid of beef and pork products. There was more flexibility under the old legislation relating to cattle than there is in the new. Then the act was so flexible that we were able actually to raise the price of butter to the producer when we decided to support the price. Later we were able to make deficiency payments on butter, and

thus maintain a lower price to the consumer without lowering the price to the producer.
The act has all these possibilities in it and many more. Deficiency payments are provided for in the act, and deficiency payments were made in connection with a number of products. That matter in itself having to do with butter was a deficiency payment. When you say to the producer, "We are going to take butter from you at 58 cents a pound", and then turn around and say, "We are going to give the butter to the wholesaler at 58 cents a pound" resulting in the consumer getting his butter at 2 to 3 cents less a pound with the government paying the carrying charges in between, that is a deficiency payment. There are dozens of ways of making deficiency payments. The law we have now makes it possible to do it in any one of those ways.
In putting this legislation before the house my hon. friend said he had examined very carefully into five different ways of putting a formula into the act, and he had decided that the one providing for a three-year base, in order to establish a basic price, was the best of all. Today he has come along and said that some people think a ten-year base is better.
With regard to that matter I am only going to say that the other day when he mentioned the matter the hon. member for Moose Mountain put in his comment and said this ten-year average was a silly proposal. I just remind the member for Moose Mountain of the fact that the first man from whom I ever heard about a ten-year average was an hon. member over in that corner of the house who is sitting looking at me now. I refer to the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Schulz).

No; a ten-year moving basis, which would not be the same years all the time. That was the submission made to the previous government, namely a ten-year basis. We gave the same answer to all those who came along with these proposals; "It does not make any difference what proposal you bring in, our act is so flexible that it is possible to utilize the suggestions in arriving at a decision as to what the support price should be".
In connection with that matter, I recall that the other day the Minister of Agriculture enumerated all the considerations which would be taken into account in putting into effect even the three-year average, and he left out what I consider to be the most important one. If I was listening carefully enough to hear all the suggestions he made, it seemed

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
to me that he did not suggest the possible importation of products into this country from outside. When we were setting support prices under the Agricultural Prices Support Act that was always one of the most important factors to be taken under consideration, and it will still remain one.
As I recall it there is only one piece of legislation that is available at the present time in order to deal with situations of that kind if you want to go further than the support act can go in dealing with them, and that is the Export and Import Permits Act. If I remember correctly that is the act upon which the official opposition of that day first decided to put on a filibuster. When that legislation was brought down following the end of the war, when it became necessary to get rid of all the proposals that had been made under the War Measures Act, we had a battle that went on for days. They did not want that legislation at all.
There are certain things which have been done since this government came into office which I do not think could have been done without the assistance of that act. It is being utilized in connection with some of these matters. In other words, the price at which you can ship products into Canada must be considered when you are putting on supports in this country.
The one with which I can illustrate the point best was dealt with effectively by the president of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture a year ago at the December conference. At that time he dealt with this matter of support prices, particularly parity prices, and he used the term "parity of income" instead of "parity prices". Then he went on to deal with the suggestion which had been made by the interprovincial farm union to the effect that there should be a price on hogs established at 100 per cent of parity basis of some $33, and that there should be a price of some $23 provided on cattle.
The president of the farm federation at that time-and he is still president-illustrated the point in his discussion at the dominion-provincial conference in December a year ago, when he said that if you were to put in that particular price as the support price in Canada, the market would be flooded in a short time by United States beef. So that question always had to be discussed or considered when supports on these products were being dealt with.
The legislation as it is made it possible for us to consider the three-year basis. As a matter of fact the three-year basis is fundamental to that legislation. We set as the basis from which we were to figure the last three

years of the war, namely 1943, 1944 and 1945, and we took that as the basis because farmers were fairly well satisfied at the time. We put right in the act the authority for comparing any support price that was brought in later on with the conditions in those three years.
Naturally it was in the middle of the three-year period that the legislation was put on the statute books, namely in 1944, and it was anticipated it would not come into effect until after the war was over. It was first applied in 1946, and so the years that were considered then were the preceding three years, 1943, 1944 and 1945. As we moved up year by year we compared three years with the last three years of the war.
I heard one of my friends back here a little while ago say, "But we never did get up to 100 per cent parity". We were supported in that, too, by farm organizations of the day. The federation said finally, after giving the matter full consideration, that the support should not be higher than 85 per cent of parity and it should not be lower than 65 per cent of parity. At a later date they changed the lower figure from 65 per cent to 70 per cent; nevertheless the fact is that on every occasion that we set a support price from that time on we checked it with the formula that had been established by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture.
There was nothing in the act that said we were compelled to do so. There was nothing in the act that said we could not do so. There was nothing in the act that said we had to abide by a three-year basis. There was nothing in the act which said we had to abide by a ten-year basis. I therefore say again that to the extent that this act says either three years or ten years, and binds anyone by it, it is not as flexible as the act that is already on the statute books, and so does not meet the conditions that may exist so well as the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
Having said that about the general statements that have been made with regard to the system which is proposed in this bill, and in view of the fact that the minister has dealt with some of the clauses seriatim, I think I should not be required to stick too closely to the rules, though I know that one of the important rules is that you do not deal with sections seriatim when you are dealing with second reading of a bill.
They could, of course, be dealt with when we are putting them through the committee, and I do not think I need say that I am not urging that anyone should not feel free to do so. But when we get into committee I suggest we can move amendments to some of these sections which are referred to. I know there will be some, and I have one in mind

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization particularly which is very important, and which has already been discussed at great length by the minister at the resolution stage, at which time I might say that none of us knew exactly what was in the bill. They were discussed again this morning on second reading. I referred to one of them when I first got to my feet, and that was the title of the bill.
The long title of the act as it now stands on the statute books is "An act for the support of the price of agricultural products during the transition from war to peace". There is a similar title to the bill which is now before the house, namely "An act to provide for the stabilization of the prices of agricultural commodities". Those two titles are intended to indicate the difference in principle between the two bills, a difference which makes it necessary to bring down a new bill.
Well, stabilization is keeping things just as much as possible where they are at the moment, and support means adding to whatever you have got. So I think if that is intended to be the difference, then the statement I made when we were discussing this at the resolution stage was quite correct and does describe the two measures quite fully.

I can quite understand why some of the critics of the bill wanted it changed and I notice that there had been changes made in it. However, the changes suggested do not cover all the points which I would suggest should be covered.
In the old legislation, as has been stated by the minister, we utilized a committee which was already in existence. It was put there for the purpose of assisting in price support measures during the war, after the war action was taken under subclause "j" to name the same persons to a committee to advise the agricultural prices support board.
The board was constituted almost entirely of persons who could be appointed under this present bill with one exception, that there is no representation of the provincial departments of agriculture under this bill.
The minister has stated "Well, there were only deputy ministers from the provincial governments on that committee". That is not true in all cases. The board had authority under that act to appoint a committee, and they did appoint a committee. That committee did not remain the same year after year; whenever farm organizations wanted a change made-either because some person who had been on it changed his mind and joined some other farm organization, or for some other reason-they came along and nominated some other representative. We accepted those nominations in every case and had the one man replaced with another. So that committee was kept up to date right along.
There is one other thing which should be stated here with respect to the committee. We never at any time suggested to the committee on what they should advise us. We never at any time asked the committee to advise us on certain things. They came here of their own volition. They asked for a date

to be set, and we set a date which was satisfactory both to them and to ourselves; we met them and they made their recommendations. Now what does this bill say?
The minister shall appoint an advisory committee. to include representation from farm organizations, consisting of a chairman and at least six, but not more than nine, other members.

I assume that is still in the amended clause as we now have it. And then it goes on to say that the members of the advisory committee may be paid for their services such remuneration and expenses as are fixed by the governor in council.
Well, I think that is the same as it was in the old act; at least the provision is the same, whether it is in the same wording I do not know. At least we had the authority to do it under either measure. When we were considering the matter of an advisory committee and of whom that advisory committee should be composed, we called in the presidents of the farm organizations and the officials who were concerned and I personally asked them this question: "Do you want to be put in the same position as the heads of the wheat board?" When they were appointed they were members of one or other of the wheat pools which are known to be farm organizations and nothing but farm organizations, but before they were on the board for two years people were referring to them in this house and outside as no longer being dirt farmers, saying they had no right to be on a board representing farmers but should be replaced by somebody else 'who did represent the dirt farmers.
I said to them, "Do you wish your representative to be paid a salary and put in that same position later on, or do you wish whoever happens to be nominated by your organization, and no matter who he is, to
come here to advise the government from time to time as a representative of that organization?" There is one other thing in these amendments which have been brought in about which I should like to say a word. We are going to have a preamble, it seems. In discussions in this house while we were in the government we were condemned in season and out of season for putting preambles in bills which, our opponents said, were intended to mean this, that and the other. I don't know just what the hon. gentleman means by that. Any parentage I have will be in the Liberal party and not in the Tory party.
In other words, we have a measure before the house which does not do all the things that could have been done under the old measure, yet there is not a single thing in it that could not have been done under the old measure without any change whatsoever excepting an additional $50 million, and it will take a lot of demonstrating to indicate that since they could not settle one problem when there was $170 million in the fund with which to settle it, they will be any more able to settle similar problems when there is $250 million there, because it will not take that much in connection with any particular project and, as I say, it could have been dealt with under the old measure.
I want to sum up by saying this. The legislation already on the statute books is the most flexible of any legislation on the statute books of any country having to do with price support, and our friends in the United States did us the honour of saying they were going to pay us the compliment of following our practice. After they had copied the idea of flexibility, our hon. friends opposite look down to the United States and say well, we guess we are in favour of flexible prices, too.
The new legislation is less flexible, but it appears to be too flexible for the C.C.F. group. They do not like flexibility in legislation of this kind, and to the extent that the Minister of Agriculture is twitting the C.C.F. with being opposed to flexible prices I am pretty much in agreement with him. We think flexible prices are appropriate to legislation

enacted for the purpose of stabilizing the return for farm products. But there is less flexibility in this act.
With regard to products, we could take in any groups of products whatsoever. We could classify them, as they are classified under the new bill, divide them into different groups and say, "We are going to deal with this one for a few months at present, and not with the other". The minister says that flexibility to this extent is a bad thing, and he is stating today he is taking it out of the act. He says we should not be in a position to put support prices on for only a few months; we should not be in a position to say, when we put a support price on hogs, that we are going to take it off in a few months' time.
Our support price on hogs is not limited to any period of a few months or to any one year. It was simply put there and it has remained there ever since the taking off of the foot-and-mouth embargo at $23 and every farmer has known it is there at $23. It is true that for the first year after the foot-and-mouth disease we did put a limit of time on it but when we dealt with it later on we took out that limit. It runs on continuously. Then, in addition to that, the act that is now on the statute books was declared in 1950 to be continuous. There is nothing limited about it. It goes right on until some other government takes it off and I am sorry to see that the some other government which is taking it off is the Conservative government whose members tell us believes in flexible prices. They propose taking off the statute books legislation that provides for the most flexible method of setting prices that has been provided anywhere. In this bill there is not so much flexibility for products and there is not so much flexibility in placing price supports as under the Agricultural Prices Support Act. My friend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) took butter as an example in order to illustrate how the act works. He said that they propose to take the average price for the last three years which would be 60 cents and put a permanent basis of 80 per cent under butter and that would be 48 cents.
What I want to say to him, and I am sure every farmer in this house will agree with me when I say it, is that when you set up in a piece of legislation a set price-call it anything you like-you give an indication to someone, usually some trader dealing with the farmer, that that is the price the government thinks ought to be paid for the commodity and the tendency will be to gravitate toward that price. For that reason we never did put a price of this kind in our supports
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization during the time we were in power and I do not think it is a good thing to put such a price in.
When you go back to the time when we put a support under butter what do you find? You find that we took into consideration all of the facts including the price of dairy products in the United States, and the price in Britain, New Zealand, Australia and everywhere. Then we worked out under the formula which was then set up what the price might be, or ought to be, here in Canada to bring 100 per cent parity. And after we worked that out we then determined what price could be put in here without finding this market flooded with commodities from somewhere else in the world and that served as the established price. It was a higher price than we had been obtaining on an average the year before. We did not say it was an average of this, that or something else. We thought the farmer needed that much in order to carry on in dairy farming and so we set it at 58 cents. Every farm organization at some time or other during the period in which that has been in effect has said that it served the farmers and served them well.
The present measure is less flexible with regard to products and prices and supports and is less flexible in its provisions with relation to the advisory committee. These were the main things mentioned by the minister when he was speaking of the act itself and the principle underlying it. Because the act that is presently on the statute books is more flexible in all three respects than the provision now before the house I am going to say again that the present act is the most flexible legislation that has ever been put on the statute books of any country to deal with price supports. Any change that is made in it in order to meet conditions will tend to make it less flexible than it had been before.
I said a few moments ago that as far as I am concerned I am voting for the measure which has been brought in. If I had an opportunity to vote for the act which presently exists I would vote for it because it is of greater benefit to the farmer. Since it has been decided by the government to repeal the present measure and bring this new bill forward I can only say there is nothing in it I would be particularly opposed to although I must comment that it does not do as much as the existing act does and I am opposed to it on that basis. But since this bill represents all this government thinks it ought to do for the farmers-and after all it said it was going to do this is what it feels is worth while doing-I am prepared to see it go on the statute books and deal with the govern-

Mr. Speaker, the bill before us to provide for the stabilization of agricultural commodities is one which to my knowledge has received more publicity than any measure which has been enacted since I have been a member of this house. It has been heralded as the main plank of the Conservative farm program; indeed, it has been described as the bill of rights for the farmer.
Right at the very outset, Mr. Speaker, I want to say that I have considered this bill and I think it is a fiasco, a monstrosity and the product of political ineptitude. I believe that one could call it a Jekyll and Hyde bill. After months of delay the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Harkness) brought into this house a measure which was supposed to be the Conservatives' key legislation to provide justice for the farmer and after bringing it in late in the dying days of the session we find that the minister is not too sure of it. In his explanation at the resolution stage the minister attempted to indicate that his officials have investigated many price formulas and supports in other countries. The events of the last week seem strange to me. After the introduction of the bill when farm organizations started to take exception to it and when members of the opposition parties expressed strong disapproval of it apparently this opposition to the proposed measure caused the backbenchers of the Tory party to do some second thinking.
I would like to ask those members sitting on the back benches in the Tory party why they did not review this proposed legislation in caucus before it was presented to the house.
More particularly I want to point out to the Minister of Agriculture that one of the firm commitments members of this party made as a political party in regard to farm policy was that the farm organizations would be called in for discussion and consultation before farm legislation with regard to farm support prices would be presented to this house. The government utterly failed to do that. Only this morning did I understand that after the bill was proposed to the house the Minister of Agriculture who was so sure of himself when he introduced the resolution decided to ask representatives of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and other farm organizations to come to Ottawa, sit down with members of the government and talk it over. Of course there was little these leaders of the farm organizations could suggest within the scope of this bill.
In the discussion that took place this morning when the minister tried to bring in
IMr. Gardiner.]

amendments to this bill he said that they did not change the principle of the bill and I think I must fully agree with him in that regard because it is a non-principle bill. There is not much principle in it and so it is pretty hard to change.
After the bill was introduced the minister, in the face of the opposition that had been voiced, decided to call in representatives of the farm organizations to try and doctor it up for the government. You can readily see the stupidity of this method of operation. I called it silly the other day and of course it is both silly and stupid. I want to warn the government that it is going to see more opposition, even with these new amendments to the bill, than any government has ever seen from farm organizations in Canada. At this moment in western Canada farm organizations are calling mass meetings with respect to this legislation. Members of this house are receiving telegrams and letters daily from farmers and farm organizations appealing to them to try to do something and asking them not to support this legislation. This proposal represents an affront to the people of Canada. Many people have lost faith in this new government which they voted for last June 10. Some things could have been done under the Agricultural Prices Support Act but with the exception of butter only on one occasion did the former government step in and do something in a real way since 1944 and that was under an emergency.
While prices of everything that the farmer had to buy were going up and the price of everything that he had to sell were going down the last Liberal government stood idly by and did nothing about it. It was not strange to me to hear the hon. member for Melville, the former minister of agriculture in the Liberal government, a party which at one time had a lot of prestige in Canada, say what he did. I am convinced that when the right hon. member said that he could do nothing but support the present legislation he truly admitted that they were bedfellows and that they agreed with the Conservative policy.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext: We do not have any bedfellows. You tried that and they kicked you out.

subtopic: MEASURE TO PROVIDE GUARANTEED PRICES FOR CERTAIN COMMODITIES, ETC.
speechtext:
If the minister who is bringing down the suggested amendments thinks that he is fooling the backbenchers in his own party-I cannot say, that is up to them-I want to say to him that he is not fooling the farm organizations. I talked to one of the leading farm organization officials this morning and he said to me: "This legislation makes me sick". It is not going to fool the western farmer; it is not going to fool

the man on the land, the man who for the past number of years has been doing a real job to feed the people of this country and the hungry people of the world. It is not going to fool the farmers. They know. They know the past Liberal government had promised to give them justice in the promises they made when the Agricultural Prices Support Act was enacted, but the government failed to do so. Under the new amendments there is nothing but pious hopes.
I want to deal briefly with the Agricultural Prices Support Act. The hon. member for Melville, of course, went into that act quite completely and I do not think I should spend too much time on it. However, I do want to say that under that legislation the former government, with the help of the revolving fund, could have supported agricultural prices so that the farmer would have received his fair share of the national income. I wish to quote from the act. This act received royal assent on August 15, 1944, and an amendment in 1950 made it continuous from April 1, 1950. The agricultural prices support board was set up under the act to:
Endeavour to ensure adequate and stable returns for agriculture . . . and to endeavour to secure a fair relationship between the returns from agriculture and those from other occupations.
These are noble sentiments, Mr. Speaker. There is a real meaning to these words if they are taken literally by any government and I can only say that the past government must have looked on this in the same way as this government appears to look on it, namely that the man on the farm should be a second-rate citizen; that he is not entitled to parity, that he is not entitled to justice as a reward for his efforts in producing foodstuffs for this country.
Of course, under the former Agricultural Prices Support Act there was an advisory board. Under the proposed act the minister is saying that they are going to have an advisory committee. The suggestion is that they will be called in and perhaps their suggestions will be listened to in formulating price support levels for the farmers. But, if past history means anything, Mr. Speaker, what assurance have we that this government, which has brought in this bill without any guarantee of a floor price in relation to parity, is going to listen to the farm organizations? What assurance have we when they have already practically ignored the farm organizations when they were drafting this bill? How can we be sure that their representations are going to be listened to? I think this bill is infamous, and it will become 96698-170
Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization more infamous for the things that it leaves out than the things it contains. In no way is it a guarantee to the farmer.
I listened very carefully, and I have gone over many times, to what the Minister of Agriculture said when he introduced this bill on December 11. He used a lot of strange words. First, he said, as reported at page 2186 of Hansard:
This is a far-reaching and important piece of legislation, perhaps the most important, in its implications, in its expected results for agriculture and its effect on the general economy, that has been considered by the Canadian parliament for many years.
Well, these are pious hopes, Mr. Speaker, because, when we discuss, as I should like to do this afternoon, the mechanics of this act, I am sure that everybody will agree it is even worse than the act we had before.
Then, the minister goes on to say that many parity price systems have been examined and that the United States price support program had been found to have many flaws. That may well be. I think almost any system of support prices or any farm program would have some flaws but let it not be forgotten that in the United States the farmers over the years have had a support price and they have had prosperity. It may well be that they have had some surpluses, but I can say that five members of the C.C.F. group went to Washington. We spent five days in the capital city and we had the good fortune to meet with many of the farm leaders of the farm bureau, and particularly of the national farmers' union of the United States, and they told us that the support prices then in force in the United States had brought prosperity to the farmers and at that time the national farmers' union was resisting the attempt of the Eisenhower government to try to break the stable price supports they had down there. Where they had brought in low flexible support prices, such as for dairy products, the support went down to 65 per cent and many dairy people were quitting the dairy industry and leaving the farm.
I am not this afternoon trying to defend what has been done under the United States prices support program but I wish to say that the prosperity of the farmer in the United States has certainly exceeded that of the Canadian farmer.
The minister tried to make a lot out of the fact that this bill has a base price based on a three year moving average. He did not say, of course, that the base price was going to be paid to the farmer. Later on in his speech he indicated that the minimum under the key commodities would be 80 per cent of the base

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization price. I have gone a little farther than the illustration which he gave to the house. In respect of butter, I have taken the period from where he left off. He took the three years on the moving average and arrived at the position where the farmer would get 48 cents in the third year under the 80 per cent formula. Now, Mr. Speaker, following that through if, in a subsequent year, butter went down 18 cents the farmer, under the 80 per cent guarantee formula, would get 43.2 cents. In the subsequent year, if it went down another 12 cents, he would get under this formula a guarantee of only 35.2 cents. Therefore, the house can see that there is really no guarantee of an adequate return so far as the price support is concerned.
These are some of the other key things which the minister indicated he hoped this bill would do. He said, as reported at page 2187 of Hansard:
First, he wants prices for his products which will cover his cost of production and leave him enough to live on;
Well, of course, this bill does nothing of the kind, Mr. Speaker. It only guarantees him at the best, under a moving average, 80 per cent of the average for the previous three years.
There is no resemblance whatever to the cost of production. Then, he says:
The farmer-he desires a sense of security in his price structure, the removal of his long-time fear that prices will fall away to nothing while his crop is growing or his livestock developing to market size.
Again, this bill fails utterly to do that very thing. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that if the government ever had the intention of introducing an adequate price support bill for agriculture, they must have completely capitulated from that stand. If the minister had taken the opportunity to call in farm organizations we would not have had this inocuous bill before us.
For the benefit of the members of this house I want first to show the reaction of the Canadian Federation of Agriculture to the proposals in this bill. This is what the federation said in making its statement on the apparent guarantees under the proposed price support bill, expressed in terms of parity as calculated by the C.F.A. formula. The average parity position of farm commodities for the past three years has been as follows: 1955, 85 per cent; 1956, 84 per cent; 1957, 82 per cent. This results in an average of 83.6 per cent. Now, 80 per cent of this three-year percentage of parity is 66.8 per cent; that is what the farmer would be guaranteed under the minister's proposal. For 1958, the guaranteed floors under the

new bill would seem to be-I am going to illustrate this by citing some of the farm products:
Per cent of Parity (C.F.A. Formula) Amount

47.7c	66 per centGood steers, Toronto . 15.3c	61 per cent
In only one case, Mr. Speaker, and that is the case of No. 1 cheese at Toronto where the amount is 27.8 cents and the percentage of parity would be 72.6 per cent, would the percentage of parity be over 70 per cent. Then, the Canadian Federation of Agriculture formula prices for 1958, percentages of parity, are as follows:

B-l hogs, Toronto	 $33.58	$23.50
In other words, under the bill which was introduced by the minister, the approved floor price would be $21.56, whereas under the C.F.A. formula of 70 per cent of parity, which is the minimum they suggest, the price would be $23.50 or 50 cents over the present support price under the Agricultural Prices Support Act.
I believe, Mr. Speaker, the time has come for political parties to stop fooling the Canadian public, particularly the Canadian farmer. This talk about no one knowing what parity prices are and not knowing how we could work out a reasonable formula having regard to parity prices should be taken out of the books because here we have in the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, 38 of the top Canadian economists, suggesting a price formula which they have put before the different governments since 1948. I feel this matter is so important I am going to put on the record their most recent recommendations regarding price support. They are as follows:
1.	Support prices should be established according to a known formula.
2.	A modernized formula for the calculation of fair relationship prices, which may be accepted as the best presently known, and which is, therefore, recommended as a guide to the setting of price supports, requires;
(a)	Calculating prices for farm products which would give them the same purchasing power per unit as in the base period 1925-29, and then-
(b)	Adjusting these individual prices so that they will have the same relationship to each other as they have had on the average during the most recent ten years.
There is your flexibility, Mr. Speaker. I continue:
These two steps should provide a set of fair relationship prices, in sound relationship to one another, but with a unit purchasing power on the average equal to the purchasing power of farm products in 1925-29.
3.	It is recommended that a formula, for use in the setting of farm price supports, be embodied in price support legislation.

Agricultural Products-Price Stabilization
4.	Support prices for the following commodities-[DOT] cheese, butter, concentrated milk products, eggs, poultry meats, bacon hogs, and wheat grown in areas outside the jurisdiction of the Canadian wheat board should be required by the price support legislation to be in effect at all times. Grains marketed by the Canadian wheat board should be supported as is suggested for the above key commodities, except that they should be administered through the agency of the wheat board.
5.	All other farm commodities should be subject to price supports as conditions may make this desirable.
6.	Support prices should not be established at less than 70 per cent of fair relationship prices and only in exceptional cases should supports be set at such a low level.
7.	Market price supports and deficiency payments should be applied on a national basis as a general rule, but regional supports, under some circumstances, should not be ruled out.
8.	Support prices to the producer must be known, and where support operations are carried on at a processing or wholesale level, producers must be assured the full benefit of such supports.
9.	The deficiency payment method of supporting incomes of producers should be applied on individual products to correct income deficiencies:
(a)	For perishable products requiring this type of support.
(b)	To supplement market price supports.
(c)	To correct income deficiencies after the product has been marketed where prices for a commodity have fallen to an unreasonably low level each year for two years; or to meet conditions such as inability to deliver production, or other special circumstances.
(d)	To be used as a guaranteed support level where the interests of consumers, continuity of supply or other special marketing problems require it.
10.	Price supports should not create incentives to production which perpetuate surplus production problems and prevent necessary and desirable production adjustments being made.
I am not going to read into the record the steps in calculating the fair relationship price, but they are here. I should think the minister should give consideration to the fact that here we have one of the leading farm organizations which has a flexible formula for parity on a basis which meets the needs of the farmers today. I am not saying I fully support it, but certainly it is something which should have been looked at before, as I say, this inocuous bill we have before us was introduced.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the other main farm organization, the interprovincial farm union council, has asked that any legislation concerning support prices be effective so that the producer would receive his fair share of the national income. I want to read into the record their submission of recent date to the government. It is this:
We appreciate that provision has been made for a federal system of price supports, but regret that it has been of little direct benefit to the producers. We believe that in order to make this policy effective, the following principles should be incorporated:
1. Price supports should be maintained at parity levels, in order that agriculture may obtain its fair share of the national income.
That is the recommendation of the interprovincial farm union council concerning its request for adequate price support.
I now want to deal with some of the statements which have been made by various members of this government. I think the time has come that this government be called before the bar of public opinion. These statements made by Conservative members in the past now require, in my opinion, to be put before this house. I want to say in particular that I believe that the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefenbaker) himself should be called before the bar of public opinion. I recognize that ordinarily in a court of law people are not called to testify against themselves. But in this case the Prime Minister has willingly done so. He has done so by speeches in the house and he has done so by speeches outside the house. I should like to read into the record some of the statements made by the Prime Minister. Speaking in 1944 on the address in regard to agricultural support prices, as recorded at page 102 of Hansard of that year the Prime Minister said this:
Reference has been made in the speech from the throne to agriculture but time does not permit my discussing that today except to say that I believe in the principle of floor prices, but like hon. members who have already spoken I ask the government what level is to be set. Is it to be a price level in accordance with present prices and subsidies? Is it to be a level that will ensure the cost of production and a reasonable profit? If it is not, it will be a denial of the farmers' due.
Those were brave words in 1944. As found at page 2023 of Hansard of March 12, 1956, the present Prime Minister of Canada said this:
The parity situation has been very thoroughly canvassed during recent years. We, in the Progressive Conservative party, tried to get some action on this matter on several occasions, but without success. One of the earliest occasions was in 1941, during the war. The last occasion when we moved an amendment regarding this question of parity prices was on March 23, 1953.
Later on he said this:
At that time I moved this amendment:
"That all the words after "that" to the end of the question be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
'in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to provide floor prices for agricultural products at such levels as to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship.' "
As found at page 2024 of Hansard of March 12, 1956 in a declaration of Conservative policy, the Prime Minister said this:
"(d) The floor price formula will be arrived at in consultation with representative producers.

We will establish a board of livestock commissioners similar to the board of grain commissioners.
We will give every legitimate encouragement to co-operative agencies whether relating to purchase, sale or credit."
As found on the same page, the Prime Minister said this:
I intend to move, sir, seconded by the hon. member for Brant-Haldimand (Mr. Charlton):
"That all the words after 'that' be struck out and the following be substituted therefor:
'in the opinion of this house consideration should be given by the government to the advisability of introducing during the present session legislation to create a parity of prices for agricultural products at levels to ensure producers a fair price-cost relationship.' "
